english.html: questing that the said creditors be satisfied out of the property that he still has at the place of Le Pin, as much from his late father Arnauld Guilhem du Tilh as from others — now possessed and occupied by Carbon Barrau his maternal uncle, whom, by reason of this, he has already sued.

This suit and demand for property which the said du Tilh was making against the said Carbon Barrau his uncle (inasmuch as the matter here was criminal and capital, where the witnesses and proofs must be entire, and clearer and more shining than the sun <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>) gave great colour to finding good the objection which the same du Tilh had, at the confrontations, proposed against the said Carbon his uncle. And it avails nothing to say that the civil law, which has rejected the testimony of one against whom we have a suit in a criminal matter, does not for that reason reprove it if the suit is brought civilly, in a civil and pecuniary matter <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>, as was the case between the said du Tilh and Barrau. For to this there are two answers. The first: that this ruling has no place where the objection is proposed by one accused of a crime <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, especially if the crime is capital, and so the head is at stake. For besides that, as we have said above, the proofs in criminal causes must be clean, must shine clearer than the sun <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>, and be exempt from all suspicion <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>, it is both certain and reasonable that where the peril is greater, affairs must be handled more warily and with greater circumspection <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. The second answer: where the suit between the parties should be for all their goods, or for the greater part, the ruling above would have no place <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup>; because a suit so weighty (for goods are esteemed as the second blood and the life of a man <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>) seems to nourish and produce I know not what enmity, and no small one <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>; and a great enemy cannot (where it is objected against him) be a witness against his

notes.citation: Code 4.19.25 (De probationibus, last law); Code 7.62 (De appellationibus et consultationibus), l. Addictos — the constitution beginning Addictos supplicio, whose place in the title is unverified (some editions carry it under C. 7.65, Quorum appellationes non recipiantur)
notes.original: l. derniere C. de proba. l. addictos. C. de ap pellatio.
notes.gloss: C. 4.19.25 (Constantine): accusers must bring proofs "supported by competent witnesses, or by the plainest documents, or by indications beyond doubt and clearer than light" — the source of Coras's "clearer than the sun".

notes.citation: Authentica Si testis in Code 4.20 (De testibus), at the end; Authenticum, seventh collation, title De testibus (Novel 90), § Si vero dicatur — chapter unverified
notes.original: Autentique ſi teſtis, à la fin. C. de teſti. P. ſi verò dica tur. de teſtib. col. vij.
notes.gloss: The Novel-derived rule that the testimony of one's adversary in a suit is excluded in criminal, not in civil, causes — the objection Coras answers.

notes.citation: Decretals, X 2.20 (De testibus), c. Testimonium and the last chapter of the title — chapter numbers unverified
notes.original: c. teſtimoniũ c. denier de te.

notes.citation: Code 4.19.25 and the law Addictos, cited above at {a}
notes.original: l. derniere & l. addictos. deſ ſus alleg.

notes.citation: Code 9.47.16 (De poenis, l. Qui sententiam); the law Addictos, Code De appellationibus, as at {a}
notes.original: l. qui ſenten t am. C. de pæ. l. addictos, C. de appel.
notes.gloss: C. 9.47.16: the judge is to pronounce no capital or severe sentence unless the accused is convicted by his own confession or by the concordant evidence of all who were examined, "so caught in the crime that he can scarcely himself deny it".

notes.citation: Digest 37.10.1 (De Carboniano edicto, l. 1), § Sed et si quis — paragraph unverified; Liber Sextus, VI 1.6.3 (De electione, c. Ubi periculum)
notes.original: l. j P, ſed, & ſi quis. D. de Carb. edict. c. vbi periculũ de electio.
notes.gloss: Ubi periculum maius intenditur, ibi procul dubio est plenius consulendum — the opening of Gregory X's constitution on the conclave (Lyon, 1274): where the peril is greater, fuller precaution is to be taken.

notes.citation: Accursius (Accurſe), the gloss on the Authentica Si testis (C. 4.20), cited above at {b}
notes.original: Accurſe en l'Autenti. ſi te ſtis, deſſus alleguee.
l. aduocati C. de aduoc. diuer. iud.
notes.gloss: Advocates who settle the doubtful fortunes of causes "provide for mankind no less than if they saved their country and their kin by battles and wounds" — the equation of goods with life.
